note: The AI prompt templates. These are the formulas from the PROMPT sheet of Book Prompt.xlsx, rewritten as plain text with {{field}} placeholders. Unlike vocab.json they are maintained by hand - they change far less often than the vocabularies, and a spreadsheet formula is a miserable place to edit a paragraph. A placeholder whose field is unset is dropped along with the sentence containing it, so a half-filled form still produces a usable prompt. Writer mode does not use this file at all - its sheets are built in writer.js from data/craft.json.

templates.label: Fiction — the story prompt
templates.summary: The main prompt. Everything the model needs to start writing.
body: The tone should be {{tone}}{{ and tone2}}.
Write it in a {{style}} style{{, with elements of style2}}.
The main themes are {{theme}}{{ and theme2}}.
Aim for around {{wordCount}} words across {{chapters}} chapters.

templates.label: Fiction — the structure instruction
templates.summary: The chapter-by-chapter working instruction. Send this straight after the story prompt.
body: Write this story in stages, chapter by chapter, followed by the ending.
Give particular attention to the first chapter: the opening has to earn the reader's attention and pull them into the world.
Organise the whole within a three-act structure - setup, confrontation, resolution - so the arc resolves rather than stops.
Build tension gradually as you approach the climax; the ending should land harder for the pressure that preceded it.
The last line matters more than any other. It is the final impression the reader takes away. Make it count.
Stop after each chapter and wait for me to prompt the next one. If a chapter needs more room than you have given it, say so rather than compressing it.

templates.label: Fiction — character generation
templates.summary: Hand this the premise and get a cast back, rather than inventing one field at a time.
body: I am writing a novel. Create a cast of characters for it - each with a name, a short description, a motivation or goal, their relationships to the others, one real strength and one real weakness.
At least one character should be defined by {{strength}}.
At least one should be undermined by {{weakness}}.
Give every character something they want that they are not going to get easily, and make sure at least two of them want incompatible things.

templates.label: Worldbuilding — the setting brief
templates.summary: Ten axes of a world. Roll them all, or set the two you care about and roll the rest.
body: Build a setting for this book with a distinct and internally consistent world.
Work out the consequences of these choices rather than just describing them. Where two of them are in tension, that tension is where the story is - say so explicitly.

templates.label: Children's book — the story prompt
templates.summary: The children's equivalent of the fiction prompt, with age band, topic and moral.
body: Write a children's book in the {{genre1}}{{ / genre2}} genre about {{childTopic}}{{ and childTopic2}}.
The tone should be {{tone}}{{ and tone2}}.
Write it in a {{style}} style{{, with elements of style2}}.
The main themes are {{childTheme}}{{ and childTheme2}}.
The moral direction should be: {{moral}}{{ Also: moral2}}
Aim for around {{wordCount}} words across {{chapters}} chapters.
Keep the vocabulary and sentence length appropriate to the age band. Do not moralise at the reader - let the moral come out of what happens.

templates.label: Children's book — character generation
templates.summary: Characters can be children, animals, magical creatures or objects.
body: I am writing a children's book. Create a cast of characters for it - they can be children, animals, magical creatures or objects. Give each a name, a short description, a motivation or goal, their relationships to the others, one strength and one weakness.
Keep every character distinguishable by how they speak, not only by what they look like.

templates.label: Non-fiction — the book brief
templates.summary: The non-fiction counterpart: argument, audience, structure and voice.
body: Write a non-fiction book in the {{nfGenre}} category.
Aim for around {{wordCount}} words across {{chapters}} chapters.
Every chapter must carry one distinct idea and advance the central argument. If two chapters make the same point, merge them. Never pad to reach a chapter count.
Before writing anything, produce the chapter outline: for each chapter, one sentence on what it argues, the example or evidence that anchors it, and the takeaway the reader leaves with. Then stop.
